title: Rules or examples
objectives: Tell a program written as rules from a model learned from examples.

screens.title: Rules a person wrote
screens.prose: A colleague writes a spam filter as one rule: **spam if it says “free”**. Here are six emails, each already marked spam or not by a person.

rows: Free entry to win a phone

screens.question: Tap every email the rule gets wrong.

hints.text: For each email, ask what the rule says, then compare with the Spam column.
C says “free” but is not spam. Which spam emails never say “free”?
The rule is wrong on C (says free, not spam), D and F (spam, no “free”).

feedback.correct: The rule gets C, D and F wrong: half of the six.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Read what the rule says for each row, then check the Spam column.

byKey.only-c: You found C, a false alarm. The rule also misses spam that never says “free”: D and F.
byKey.missed-c: You found the missed spam, D and F. C says “free” and is not spam, so the rule flags it wrongly.
byKey.r0: You tapped A. It says “free” and is spam, so the rule gets it right.
byKey.r1: You tapped B. It has no “free” and is not spam, so the rule gets it right.
byKey.r4: You tapped E. No “free” and not spam: the rule is right there.

explain.text: A rule a person writes catches only what that person thought of. This one flags C wrongly and misses D and F. That is 3 mistakes in 6 emails.

screens.title: Try your own rule
screens.prose: Now choose a rule yourself. Each one looks at a single column. The caption counts the mistakes on the six emails.

rows: Free entry to win a phone

state.caption: Says “free”: wrong on C, D, F, so 3 mistakes.

frames.caption: Says “free”: wrong on C, D, F, so 3 mistakes.
Links at least 1: wrong on C, E, so 2 mistakes.
Links at least 5: no mistakes on these six.
Links at least 8: wrong on A, D, F, so 3 mistakes.

screens.question: Which rule makes no mistakes on these six emails?

options.text: Spam when links are at least 5
Spam when it says “free”
options.why: That rule made 3 mistakes: C, D and F. Slide back to it and read the caption.

options.text: Spam when links are at least 8
options.why: With 8 as the bar, A, D and F slip through: 3 mistakes.

hints.text: Slide through the rules and read each caption.
Links at least 5 is the only rule with no mistakes.

feedback.correct: Links at least 5 gets all six right.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Slide to each rule and read its mistake count.

explain.text: Counting links does better than looking for one word on these six. You found that by trying rules and counting mistakes. A program can do the same trying for us.

canvas.caption: Links at least 5: no mistakes on these six.

screens.title: Found, not written
screens.prose: The rule **spam when links are at least 5** was not written by a person. A program was shown ten emails, each marked spam or not, and it found the rule. A **program** is rules a person wrote. A **model** is a rule found from examples. **Machine learning** is the finding.
screens.question: Tap the box that the examples choose.

hints.text: In the bottom row, which box comes out of the learning?
The learner reads the examples and hands something on.
The learner turns the examples into the model, which then gives answers.

feedback.correct: The examples choose the model. Nobody writes it by hand.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Follow the bottom row from the examples to the answer.

byKey.rules: You tapped the rules in the top row. A person writes those; no examples are involved.
byKey.learner: The learner is the program that does the finding. It is the same whatever the examples; what it produces changes.
byKey.examples: The examples are what goes in. The box they shape comes later in the row.
byKey.person: A person writes rules in the top row. In machine learning the rule is found instead.
byKey.answer1: That answer comes from rules a person wrote.
byKey.answer2: The answer comes out of the model. Tap the box that gives it.

explain.text: The examples go into the learner, and out comes the model. Show it different examples and you get a different model. The learner itself does not change.

screens.title: Sort the tasks
screens.prose: Five jobs: add VAT at 20% to a price; pick a person's tax band from their income; spot a cat in a photo; read handwritten digits; score a loan's risk of default from past loans.
screens.question: Drag a chip onto each job: write the rules, or learn from examples.

hints.text: Could you write the exact rule down in a sentence or two?
VAT and tax bands are set by law, so the rules are written down.
VAT and Tax band take Write the rules; the other three take Learn from examples.

feedback.correct: Exact written rules for VAT and tax bands; examples for cats, handwriting and loan risk.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask whether anyone could write the full rule down.

explain.text: When the exact rule is known, write it. When nobody can write it but we have labelled examples, learn it. Cats, handwriting and loan risk are the second kind.

screens.title: New examples, new rule
screens.prose: The same program is shown ten emails from a different office. It returns the rule **spam when links are at least 3**.
screens.question: What made the rule change from 5 to 3?

options.text: The examples: a different set of emails chose a different number
Someone rewrote the program for the new office
options.why: The program is the same one. Only the emails it was shown are new.

options.text: The program picks the number at random
options.why: It picks the number that fits its examples, so the same emails give the same number.

options.text: The first rule must have been wrong
options.why: Each rule fits its own office's emails. Neither is wrong for the emails it saw.

hints.text: What is different between the two runs?
Only the emails differ, so they chose the number.

feedback.correct: The examples chose the number. Same program, new emails, new rule.
feedback.generic: Not quite. The program did not change between the two runs.

explain.text: A model's numbers come from its examples. Ten other emails pushed the bar from 5 down to 3. The learner was the same both times.

screens.title: Does it think?
screens.prose: Your bank sends a real statement with 6 links. The filter marks it spam. A friend says: “The model read it, thought about it, and judged it a scam.”
screens.question: What did the model really do?

options.text: It counted 6 links, saw 6 is at least 5, and said spam
It read the email and judged it, as a person would
options.why: The model never reads words. Its only rule is links at least 5, found from ten emails.

options.text: It knows the bank's emails look like scams
options.why: It knows nothing about banks. It compares one number, the link count, with 5.

options.text: It learned to spot scams from millions of emails
options.why: It saw ten emails, and all it took from them was the number 5.

hints.text: What does the model's rule look at?
Its whole rule is “spam when links are at least 5”. Check 6 against it.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Apply the model's one rule to this email.

byKey.think: You gave the model a mind. It applies one rule it found: links at least 5. This email has 6, so it says spam.

explain.text: A model only finds a rule that fits its examples. This one checks whether links are at least 5, so the bank's email with 6 links is flagged. It is a rule with a number in it, not a person thinking.

screens.title: When learning is a waste
screens.prose: Learning needs many examples and still makes mistakes. Some jobs have a perfect rule already.
screens.question: Which job gains nothing from learning?

options.text: Converting pounds to pence
Spotting a forged signature
options.why: Nobody can write a full rule for forgeries. Labelled examples help here.

options.text: Guessing tomorrow's number of shop visitors
options.why: No exact rule exists. Past days with their visitor counts are examples to learn from.

options.text: Turning speech into text
options.why: Speech varies too much for written rules. Recordings with their text are the examples.

hints.text: Which job has a rule you could write in five words?
Multiply by 100: the rule for pence is exact.

feedback.correct: Pounds to pence is multiply by 100: exact, with no examples needed.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Look for the job whose exact rule is already known.

explain.text: Multiplying by 100 is right every time. A model learned from examples would only be close. When an exact rule exists, write it.

screens.title: A model is a machine
screens.prose: A model is a function machine, as in functions l1: inputs go in, an output comes out. Ours is $$f(\text{links}) = \begin{cases} \text{spam} & \text{if links} \ge 5 \\ \text{not spam} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$ The shape of the rule is chosen by people. The number in it, 5, was chosen by the examples.
screens.question: An email arrives with 4 links. What is $f(4)$?

options.text: Not spam
Spam
options.why: You read the rule as “more than 3”. The rule asks for at least 5 links, and 4 is below 5.

hints.text: Is 4 at least 5?
4 is below 5, so the rule gives not spam.

feedback.correct: 4 is below 5, so $f(4)$ is not spam.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare 4 with the number in the rule.

explain.text: The machine compares the input with its number, 5. Since 4 is below 5, the output is not spam.

screens.title: A fund's signal
screens.prose: A fund keeps 2,000 past trades. Each has a signal value at the time and whether the trade made money. A program tries cut-offs. It keeps **trade when the signal is above 0.3**, which made money on most of them.
screens.question: Which part did the examples choose?

options.text: The cut-off, 0.3
The 2,000 trades
options.why: The trades are the examples themselves, what goes in. They chose something.

options.text: The idea of using a signal
options.why: People chose to use a signal. The examples only set the number in the rule.

options.text: Whether the next trade makes money
options.why: That is what the rule is for. It is not known until after the trade.

hints.text: Which number would change if the fund had a different 2,000 trades?
The cut-off 0.3 is the number the examples chose.

feedback.correct: The examples chose 0.3, as the emails chose 5.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Look for the number inside the rule.

explain.text: Examples in, rule out: past trades went in and the cut-off 0.3 came out. A bank's fraud filter is the same, with past card payments marked fraud or not. In both, people pick the shape and the data pick the number.

ideas: A program follows rules a person wrote; a model follows a rule found from examples.
Machine learning is the finding: new examples give a new rule from the same learner.
When an exact rule is known, write it; learn only when nobody can write the rule.

formula.name: A model
formula.note: People choose the shape of the rule. The examples choose its numbers.

summary.trap: A model does not think. It applies a rule, such as links at least 5, that fitted its examples.

quiz.prose: A shop's till adds 20% VAT to every price.
quiz.question: Is the till's VAT step a program or a model?

options.text: A program: a person wrote the exact rule
A model: it learned 20% from past receipts
options.why: The 20% is set by law and typed in by a person. Nothing was learned from examples.

feedback.correct: A person wrote it, so it is a program.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask where the 20% came from.

explain.text: The rule is known exactly and was typed in. That makes it a program. A model's rule is found from examples instead.

quiz.prose: Five emails have 0, 2, 4, 6 and 8 links. Only the ones with 6 and 8 links are spam.
quiz.question: The rule **spam when links are at least 4** is applied. How many of the five does it get wrong?

feedback.correct: Only the email with 4 links is wrong: flagged, but not spam.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Apply the rule to each email in turn.

byKey.right-count: 4 is how many it gets right. The question asks how many it gets wrong: 5 − 4 = 1.

explain.text: The rule flags 4, 6 and 8. The emails with 6 and 8 are spam, but 4 is not. So the rule gets 1 email wrong.

quiz.prose: A weather app was shown 5,000 past days, each with the morning's air pressure and whether it rained. It now says rain when the pressure is below 1,005.
quiz.question: Which statement is true?

options.text: The number 1,005 was chosen by the past days
The app understands weather the way a forecaster does
options.why: It compares one number with 1,005. That is a rule found from examples, not understanding.

options.text: 1,005 is the exact rule for rain
options.why: It is the cut-off that fitted the 5,000 days best. Other days could pick another number.

options.text: A person typed 1,005 into the app
options.why: No person picked it. The program found it from the 5,000 days.

feedback.correct: The past days chose the number.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask what chose the 1,005.

explain.text: The app is a model: its rule's number came from examples. A different set of days could have given a different cut-off.
